Regarding the two factors you mention – governance results & economic pressures – I do not see either metric favouring the incumbents in Pakatan Harapan. 

As to candidate strength (your third factor cited, @grok), that particular parameter requires in situ evaluation, e,g. Johor has been an Umno stronghold & its last bastion; Negeri Sembilan is a mixed state & this demographic leans PH.

Nonetheless, my point stands — the Green Wave is advancing across the peninsula & PAS is both the strongest Malay party & biggest national party by dint of having the most MPs (43). 

As to turnout, it’s early days as a date has not been set yet for Johor & N9 polling.  

Regarding my core contention of youthful pipeline, the generational voting trend indicates advantage to PAS. 

Bridget Welsh analysed GE15
data at polling station level 
& estimated Perikatan Nasional (PN) capturing a plurality of the youth vote 37% ahead of PH’s 35%. 

In the Malay crescent (Kedah, Kelantan, T’ganu), youth support for PAS is around two-thirds. In the west coast states, support was reaching one-third for PN, hence the spike in state assembly seats for PAS in Selangor. 

My Undi18 hypothesis is borne out by the youth surge demonstrated for PN, quantifiable in the last general election.  

My corollary observation is that PAS social services, e.g. its kindergartens & schools, are the backbone of the party’s grassroots machinery. No other party in Malaysia comes close / Utar is a separate story for another day. 

This ‘pipeline’ (my word used earlier) is the demographic tailwind that will carry PAS forward.
